title: Salih and the she-camel
hookLine: Thamud are given a she-camel as a sign and told to let her graze (7:73–79)

lines: A SIGN THAT WAS AN ANIMAL.
cards: In northwest Arabia, near the town of al-Ula, enormous tombs are carved straight into sandstone cliffs, their doorways cut like temple fronts.
Muslim tradition has long linked this region, al-Hijr, with the people of Thamud. Archaeologists date the tombs standing there now to the Nabataeans, a later people.
But the Qur'an says Thamud, too, carved homes out of mountains. And it tells of a sign sent to them that wasn't a wall or a tower at all. It was an animal.

teach.b: Verse seventy-three: to Thamud, their brother Salih. Same message as Hud: worship Allah, you have no god but Him. Then he points to a sign: this is the she-camel of Allah.
Let her eat in Allah's earth, and don't touch her with harm, or a painful punishment will take you.

teach.h: NAQAT ALLAH — THE CAMEL OF GOD.
teach.b: The Arabic is naqat Allah, the camel of God, a phrase that gives an ordinary animal enormous dignity.

teach.h: A DAY TO DRINK, A DAY FOR YOU.
teach.b: Surah twenty-six adds that the water was to be shared: a day for her to drink, and a day for the people. The test was almost too simple. Leave her alone.

Share the well. Salih reminds them of their blessings: Allah made them successors after 'Ad, with plains for palaces and mountains to carve into homes. The proud chiefs mock the poorer people who believed.
Then, verse seventy-seven, they hamstring the she-camel and say to Salih, bring on what you threaten. Surah ninety-one says it was done by the most wretched of them, while the people went along.
The earthquake took them, and morning found them fallen in their homes.
When the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ later passed through al-Hijr on the way to Tabuk, Bukhari reports he told his companions not to enter the dwellings of those punished except in tears.
Elsewhere, hadith tell of a man forgiven for giving water to a thirsty dog, and a woman punished for starving a cat. In this tradition, how people treat an animal is never a small thing.

how: Muslims honor Salih as a prophet sent to Thamud; his story is taught alongside hadith on kindness to animals, and teachers recall the reports about the Prophet passing al-Hijr.

games.q: you're one of Thamud. the she-camel drinks from your well on her day. what does Salih ask?
o: leave her and share the water, a day each.
games.why: let her eat in Allah's earth and touch her not with harm. they hamstrung her instead, and the earthquake came.

practice: Picture an animal you'll likely cross today, a pigeon on the sidewalk, a neighbor's dog, a cat in an alley, a bee at a window, going about its business.
Then picture yourself simply letting it be, not chasing, shooing or swatting, maybe leaving a little water out, and hold that picture of an animal left in peace.

wordCard.voice: Salih. A prophet sent to Thamud, and a sign, a she-camel, that asked only to be left in peace and given her share of water. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: a she-camel. naqat Allah: the she-camel of God (7:73).

carryVoice: Your line: leave her to graze. The whole test was one animal and a shared well. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 2363 (the dog given water); Sahih al-Bukhari 3318 (the cat)
